paragraphs: The 9A2.10 is a low-volume, high-performance engine. Prices vary significantly by sub-variant - the 718 GT4 RS and 911 GT3 units carry a premium over the 718 GTS 4.0. failures.title: Porsche 9A2.10 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Connecting Rod Failure - 2021 production batch (718 GT4, Spyder, GTS 4.0)
items.whatHappens: A defective batch of engine connecting rods was identified in 2021 718 models equipped with the 4.0-litre flat-six. The rods may crack and loosen, potentially leading to sudden engine failure, stalling, and in extreme cases, fire risk. Porsche issued a stop-sale and recall on approximately 190 UK/EU vehicles.
items.repairVsReplace: If the engine has already suffered connecting rod failure, a full replacement is almost always required - Porsche replaced affected engines under warranty. For cars outside the recall batch, no preventative action is currently available beyond regular oil analysis. Read our full engine failure guide

items.title: Oil Leaks and Gasket Failures
items.whatHappens: Like many Porsche flat-six engines, the 9A2.10 can develop oil leaks from valve cover gaskets and oil cooler seals. These are not catastrophic if caught early, but can lead to low oil pressure and eventual bearing failure if ignored. Porsche specialist workshops report this as the most common service-age failure on higher-mileage 9A2 units.
items.repairVsReplace: Gasket replacement is a straightforward but labour-intensive repair (8-12 hours). If oil starvation has occurred due to prolonged low oil level, bearing damage may necessitate a full rebuild or replacement.

items.title: Water Pump and Cooling System Issues
items.whatHappens: The water pump and associated cooling system components are a known wear point on modern Porsche flat-six engines. Coolant leaks, water pump failure, and thermostat issues can lead to overheating and potential cylinder head damage if not addressed promptly.
items.repairVsReplace: Water pump replacement is a routine service item (£800-£1,500 at an independent specialist). If overheating has occurred, cylinder head inspection and potential rebuild costs escalate significantly.

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2021 9A2.10 units (after the connecting rod recall was addressed) are considered robust for a high-performance naturally aspirated engine. The 992-generation 911 GT3 units (2021+) benefit from further refinements and have fewer reported issues than the 718 4.0-litre batch.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the 9A2.10
variants.intro: The 9A2.10 is a specific 4.0-litre naturally aspirated variant within Porsche's modular 9A2 engine family. Unlike the turbocharged 3.0-litre 9A2 units (fitted to 991.2 and 992 Carrera models), the 9A2.10 is distinguished by its 4.0-litre displacement, naturally aspirated induction, and higher 9,000 rpm redline in GT3 applications. Where the code appears: - On the engine block - stamped on the left-hand side near the oil filter housing - On the V5C registration document (engine number field) - Via Porsche VIN decoder - the 8th character of the VIN indicates engine type Commonly confused codes: - 9A2 evo - the six-cylinder turbocharged 3.0-litre unit fitted to 992 Carrera and Carrera S models; fundamentally different induction and power delivery - 9A1 - the previous-generation naturally aspirated 3.8L/4.0L flat-six (991.1 GT3, 981 GT4); different engine architecture and timing chain design

relatives.description: the 3.8L and 4.0L naturally aspirated flat-six that powered the 991.1 GT3 and 981 GT4. The 9A2.10 replaced it with a modular architecture, but the Metzger is still revered for its robustness and is more easily rebuildable.

the current evolution of the modular flat-six, with revised fuel injection and emissions systems. It does not fundamentally change the core architecture but adds hybrid assistance in some applications.

the turbocharged 3.0-litre unit fitted to 991.2 and 992 Carrera models. It shares the same basic block design but uses forced induction, smaller displacement, and a different crank/rod assembly. If you have a turbocharged 911, this is not your engine.
not yet; the 9A2.10 remains the only naturally aspirated 4.0L in the family. No cross-brand sharing applies.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement 9A2.10 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used 9A2.10 can make sense for a 718 or 911 owner facing an out-of-warranty failure, but only if the engine comes with documented service history and - critically - proof that it is not from the 2021 connecting rod recall batch. The primary risk is hidden oil starvation damage from previous track use.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper 9A2.10 recon addresses the engine's specific failure points: connecting rod inspection/replacement (for 2021-era units), full gasket and seal replacement to address oil leaks, and a complete cooling system overhaul including water pump and thermostat. This is the right call for a high-value 718 GT4 or 911 GT3 where the car's value justifies the spend.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild is justified for the 9A2.10 when the engine has suffered catastrophic failure (connecting rod failure, bearing seizure) and the original block is still viable. An upgraded rebuild should include billet connecting rods (aftermarket), upgraded oil pump, and enhanced cooling - turning a known weakness into a track-ready strength.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** Fitting through the EnginesMarket network ensures your replacement 9A2.10 is supplied by a vetted Porsche specialist with a minimum 12-month warranty. Supply-only or full supply & fit available nationwide.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The 9A2.10 is fitted to some of Porsche's most valuable modern sports cars. A 718 Cayman GT4 holds £60,000-£110,000 depending on spec and mileage; a 992 GT3 commands £150,000-£210,000. A £35,000-£45,000 replacement engine is a significant but justifiable expense relative to the vehicle's value. For a high-mileage 718 GTS 4.0 at the lower end of the value spectrum (£50,000-£60,000), evaluate the car's overall condition and service history before committing to a full replacement - a rebuild may be more cost-effective.

items.question: What are the common problems with the 9A2.10 engine?
items.answer: The most significant known issue is connecting rod failure affecting a 2021 production batch of 718 models - Porsche issued a stop-sale and recall for around 190 UK/EU cars. Other common failures include oil leaks from gaskets and seals (30k-60k miles) and water pump/cooling system wear (40k-70k miles). The connecting rod defect can cause sudden engine seizure and fire risk - check if your car was part of the recall. Oil leaks are not catastrophic if caught early, but can lead to bearing failure if oil pressure drops. Cooling system issues are routine on higher-mileage units and are best addressed preventatively.

items.question: Which Porsche models use the 9A2.10 engine?
items.answer: The 9A2.10 is fitted to the 718 Boxster GTS 4.0 and Spyder, 718 Cayman GT4, GT4 RS and GTS 4.0, and the 992-generation 911 GT3 and GT3 RS (both 992.1 and 992.2). It is the flagship naturally aspirated flat-six for Porsche's sports car range. The engine is not used in any other brand; it is Porsche-specific. Production years span from 2016 to present, with the 718 units arriving from 2020 and the 992 GT3 from 2021. The 911 GT3 variants are the highest-power applications (502-520hp).

items.question: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt 9A2.10?
items.answer: A used 9A2.10 can be viable if it has full service history and is proven to be outside the 2021 recall batch - but the risk of hidden track damage is real. Reconditioned is the safest option for a high-value car, as it addresses all known failure points (rods, gaskets, cooling). A full rebuild is justified if your original block is still sound and you want upgraded internals for track use. For a 718 GTS 4.0 with lower value, a rebuild may be more cost-effective than a full reconditioned unit. Always insist on a warranty of at least 12 months for any replacement.

items.question: How do I confirm my car has the 9A2.10 engine and not another variant?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on the left-hand side of the block near the oil filter housing. It also appears on your V5C registration document and can be decoded from the VIN (8th character). The 9A2.10 is uniquely identified by its 4.0L displacement and naturally aspirated induction - if your car has a turbocharger, it is a different engine. Common confusions include the 9A2 turbo 3.0L and the older 9A1 3.8L/4.0L. Enter your registration above for a definitive fitment check.

items.question: How long do 9A2.10 engines typically last?
items.answer: With proper maintenance, a 9A2.10 can exceed 100,000 miles. However, track use and repeated high-RPM operation can shorten lifespan significantly. The biggest longevity factor is oil condition - frequent changes (every 5,000-6,000 miles or annually) and using the correct Porsche-approved oil are critical. The connecting rod recall was a manufacturing defect, not a wear issue. Regular cooling system servicing and gasket checks are recommended from 40,000 miles.
